subtype: Adult offers words to a child [Observer]
passage:
Himani stomped into the kitchen and threw her doll on the floor.
"Himani," said Sarita Maasi, putting down the knife. "Your face looks cross. Are you upset?"
Himani's lip pushed out. "No."
"Hmm. Your fists are tight too." Maasi knelt down. "Is it cross? Or sad? Or both?"
Himani looked at her fists. "Cross," she said slowly. "Chintu took my crayons."
"Ah. That's a cross feeling, all right."
"And sad," Himani added. "He said my picture was ugly."
"Cross and sad. Thank you for telling me." Maasi held out her arms, and Himani walked into them.

qa.q: What did Chintu take?
qa.a: Himani's crayons.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling beneath the stomping, once the words came?
qa.a: Himani was cross that Chintu took the crayons and sad that Chintu called the picture ugly.

qa.q: What did Sarita Maasi do that helped Himani name the feelings?
qa.a: Maasi noticed Himani's face and fists and offered simple words, cross or sad, without pushing, so Himani could pick the right ones.

qa.q: How might Sarita Maasi feel when Himani walks into her arms?
qa.a: Sarita Maasi would probably feel warm and relieved, glad the gentle naming helped Himani open up. 🤍

grounding: An aunt notices a five-year-old's cross face and offers simple feeling words until the child can name being cross and sad.

passage: Teacher's note, KG-B, Monday. Suraj Menon. Wasim (5) spent the morning kicking the table leg and pushing his tray away. When I asked what was wrong, he said 'Nothing!' and hid his face. I didn't press. Later I sat beside him and said, 'Your face looks cross, and your feet are kicking. Are you upset?' He was quiet, then said, 'Upset. Ammi didn't drop me.' I said, 'You feel upset because you missed Ammi this morning.' He nodded and stopped kicking. Next: keep naming feelings aloud for Wasim, simply and without pressure, and use the feelings-faces chart at circle time.

qa.q: What did Wasim do during the morning?
qa.a: Kicked the table leg and pushed the tray away.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling, once a word was found?
qa.a: Wasim felt upset because Ammi hadn't dropped him at school that morning.

qa.q: Why did Suraj Menon's second try work better than asking what was wrong?
qa.a: Describing Wasim's face and kicking and offering one word gave Wasim something to agree with, instead of a big question to answer.

qa.q: How might Wasim's Ammi feel reading about this?
qa.a: Ammi might feel a pang knowing Wasim missed her, and glad the teacher helped Wasim put it into words.

grounding: A teacher names a kicking five-year-old's cross face and helps him find the word upset, without pressure.

subtype: Adult offers words to a child [Observer]
passage: At the anganwadi in the Goan village, the children were drawing fish. Maria, five, scribbled so hard that her crayon snapped. She sat with her arms folded and her bottom lip out. Dilnaz Teacher crouched beside her. 'Maria, your face looks cross. Are you upset?' Maria shrugged. Dilnaz waited, then pointed at the faces chart on the wall: happy, sad, cross, scared. 'Which one is like you?' Maria looked for a long time. She tapped 'cross,' then 'sad.' 'My fish looks bad,' she whispered. 'Cross and sad about your fish,' said Dilnaz Teacher. 'Shall we draw another together?' Maria unfolded her arms.

qa.q: Which faces were on the chart?
qa.a: Happy, sad, cross, scared.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when she folded her arms?
qa.a: Maria was cross and sad that her fish drawing looked bad, even though she couldn't say it at first.

qa.q: Why was pointing at the faces chart a good choice after Maria shrugged?
qa.a: It gave Maria pictures to choose from when words were hard, so Maria could name cross and sad without pressure.

qa.q: How might the other children see Maria's snapped crayon?
qa.a: They might think Maria was just being naughty, not knowing she felt cross and sad about her fish.

grounding: A village teacher uses gentle words and a faces chart to help a cross five-year-old name her feelings.

subtype: Adult offers words to a child [Observer]
passage:
At the playground in Lisbon, a bigger boy grabbed the swing just as Nour reached it. Nour, five, stomped to the bench and sat with her arms crossed, kicking the sand.
Her mother, Camila, sat beside her. "Your eyebrows are all squished together. Are you feeling cross?"
Nour kicked harder. "No."
"Okay." Camila waited, watching the pigeons.
After a while Nour said, "He took it. I was first."
"Ah. That's annoying."
"I'm angry," Nour said, trying the word. "Very angry."
"That makes sense."
When the boy left, Nour ran to the swing.

qa.q: What did the bigger boy grab?
qa.a: He grabbed the swing.

qa.q: What did Nour mean when she said, 'I'm angry,' after first saying no?
qa.a: She had found a word for the hot feeling after the swing was taken; saying it showed she now knew she felt cross because she had been first.

qa.q: Which of Camila's choices helped Nour find the word, and why?
qa.a: Naming what she saw on Nour's face and then waiting, without pushing when Nour said no, gave Nour time to find the feeling herself.

qa.q: What would change if Camila had just said, 'Stop sulking'?
qa.a: Nour would probably have felt told off and stayed stuck in her anger, without learning a word for it.

grounding: It shows a parent naming what she sees on her child's face and waiting without pressure, helping the child put a word to her feeling.

subtype: Adult offers words to a child [Observer]
passage:
At swimming class, Vijay, five, stood at the edge of the small pool, arms folded, lips pressed tight.
Jyotsna Teacher waded over and crouched so her eyes were level with his. "Your shoulders are up near your ears. Are you scared? Or cross? Or both?"
Vijay looked at the water. "Scared," he whispered. "And a bit cross. Everybody's looking."
"Scared and a bit cross. Two feelings. Thank you for telling me." She patted the top step. "Want to just sit here today?"
Vijay sat on the top step, feet in the water.

qa.q: Where did Vijay sit at the end?
qa.a: He sat on the top step, feet in the water.

qa.q: What was Vijay worried about at the pool's edge?
qa.a: He was scared of the water and a bit cross because everybody was looking at him.

qa.q: How did Jyotsna Teacher's approach help Vijay?
qa.a: She named his raised shoulders and offered a few words to choose from without pressure, which let Vijay name two feelings and then try sitting on the step.

qa.q: How might the other children see Vijay sitting on the step?
qa.a: They may not think much of it at all, since he is in the water too, which could make Vijay feel less watched next time.

grounding: It shows a teacher gently offering feeling words to a young child so he can name what he feels, without pressure.
